(III) A flexible loop of irregular shape carrying current when located in an external magnetic field, changes to a circular shape. Give reason.
(ii) A galvanometer of resistance G is converted into a voltmeter to measure up to V volts, by connecting a resistance \(\mathrm{R_1}\) in series with the coil. If \(\mathrm{R_1}\) is replaced by \(\mathrm{R_2}\), then it can only measure up to \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V}}{2}\) volt. Find the value of the resistance \(\mathrm{R_3}\) (in terms of \(\mathrm{R_1}\) and \(\mathrm{R_2}\)) needed to convert it into a voltmeter that can read up to 2 V.
rows.solution:
(i) (I) AMPERE'S CIRCUITAL LAW. The line integral of the magnetic field around any closed loop equals \(\mu_{0}\) times the net current threading that loop:
\(\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_{0}I_{e}\)
where \(\vec{B}\) is the magnetic field, \(d\vec{l}\) an element of the closed path, called the Amperian loop, and \(I_{e}\) the TOTAL current passing through any surface bounded by that loop.
(II) WHY THE FIELD OUTSIDE A LONG SOLENOID APPROACHES ZERO. As the solenoid is made longer, its turns approximate a continuous CYLINDRICAL SHEET of current. The field lines produced by each turn then have to complete their return path over a greater and greater length, so they spread out over a larger and larger volume outside. The outside field, being the same flux spread through an ever-growing cross-section, weakens, and in the ideal infinite limit it becomes zero, with all the flux confined inside.
(III) WHY AN IRREGULAR FLEXIBLE LOOP BECOMES CIRCULAR. The forces on a current-carrying loop in an external field act so as to increase the flux linked with it, and for a given PERIMETER, which is fixed since the wire cannot stretch, the shape enclosing the GREATEST AREA is the circle. The loop therefore springs outwards into a circular shape, maximising the flux through it.
(ii) A galvanometer of resistance G and full-scale current \(I_{g}\) becomes a voltmeter of range V when a series resistance R is chosen so that \(V = I_{g}(G + R)\).
FIRST CASE, range V with \(R_{1}\):
\(\dfrac{V}{I_{g}} = R_{1} + G \qquad\text{...(1)}\)
SECOND CASE, range \(\dfrac{V}{2}\) with \(R_{2}\):
\(\dfrac{V}{2I_{g}} = R_{2} + G \qquad\text{...(2)}\)
Multiplying (2) by 2 and subtracting (1) eliminates the voltage:
\(2R_{2} + 2G - R_{1} - G = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad G = R_{1} - 2R_{2}\)
THIRD CASE, the required range 2V with \(R_{3}\):
\(\dfrac{2V}{I_{g}} = R_{3} + G \qquad\text{...(3)}\)
From (1), \(\dfrac{2V}{I_{g}} = 2(R_{1} + G)\), so
\(R_{3} = 2R_{1} + 2G - G = 2R_{1} + G = 2R_{1} + (R_{1} - 2R_{2})\)
\(R_{3} = 3R_{1} - 2R_{2}\)

rows.stem:
(i) Explain with the help of a labelled ray diagram the formation of final image by an astronomical telescope at infinity. Write the expression for its magnifying power.
(ii) The total magnification produced by a compound microscope is 20. The magnification produced by the eyepiece is 5. When the microscope is focussed on a certain object, the distance between the objective and eyepiece is observed to be 14 cm. Calculate the focal lengths of the objective and the eyepiece. (Given that the least distance of distinct vision = 25 cm)
rows.solution:
(i) ASTRONOMICAL TELESCOPE, final image at infinity, which is the normal adjustment.
RAY DIAGRAM: draw a converging objective of large focal length \(f_{0}\) on the left and a converging eyepiece of short focal length \(f_{e}\) on the right, separated so that the focal points between them COINCIDE. Take a parallel beam from a distant object arriving at a small angle \(\alpha\) to the axis. The objective brings it to a real, inverted image A'B' in its focal plane. Since that plane is also the focal plane of the eyepiece, the eyepiece sends the light out as a parallel beam, now making a larger angle \(\beta\) with the axis, and the final image is formed AT INFINITY. Mark arrows on every ray.
The eye is relaxed in this arrangement, which is why it is preferred for prolonged observation.
MAGNIFYING POWER is the ratio of the angle subtended at the eye by the final image to that subtended by the object:
\(m = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{f_{0}}{f_{e}}\)
and the length of the tube is \(f_{0} + f_{e}\). A large objective focal length and a short eyepiece focal length together make a powerful telescope.
(ii) The final image here is at the LEAST DISTANCE OF DISTINCT VISION, \(D = 25\) cm, since the total magnification is quoted with the eyepiece magnifying 5 times.
EYEPIECE. For an image at D,
\(m_{e} = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f_{e}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 5 = 1 + \dfrac{25}{f_{e}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f_{e} = \dfrac{25}{4} = 6{\cdot}25\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Locating its object, with \(v_{e} = -25\) cm:
\(\dfrac{1}{-25} - \dfrac{1}{u_{e}} = \dfrac{4}{25} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u_{e} = -5\ \mathrm{cm}\)
OBJECTIVE. The intermediate image lies 5 cm in front of the eyepiece, and the two lenses are 14 cm apart, so
\(v_{0} = 14 - 5 = 9\ \mathrm{cm}\)
The objective's magnification is the total divided by the eyepiece's:
\(m_{0} = \dfrac{20}{5} = 4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left|\dfrac{v_{0}}{u_{0}}\right| = 4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u_{0} = -\dfrac{9}{4}\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Applying the lens formula:
\(\dfrac{1}{f_{0}} = \dfrac{1}{9} - \left(-\dfrac{4}{9}\right) = \dfrac{5}{9} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad f_{0} = \dfrac{9}{5} = 1{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{cm}\)
The objective has a focal length of \(1{\cdot}8\) cm and the eyepiece \(6{\cdot}25\) cm. The objective being much the shorter is the signature of a MICROSCOPE, and is exactly the reverse of the telescope in part (i).

rows.stem:
(i) Two coherent light waves, each of intensity \(\mathrm{I_0}\) superpose each other and produce interference pattern on a screen. Obtain the expression for the resultant intensity at a point where the phase difference between the waves is \(\phi\). Write its maximum and minimum possible values.
(ii) In a single slit diffraction experiment, the aperture of the slit is 3 mm and the separation between the slit and the screen is \(1{\cdot}5\) m. A monochromatic light of wavelength 600 nm is normally incident on the slit. Calculate the distance of (I) first order minimum, and (II) second order maximum, from the centre of the screen.
rows.solution:
(i) Let the two coherent waves arriving at a point be
\(y_{1} = a\cos\omega t, \qquad y_{2} = a\cos(\omega t + \phi)\)
each of amplitude a, so that each alone would give intensity \(I_{0} \propto a^{2}\).
By the principle of SUPERPOSITION the displacements add:
\(y = y_{1} + y_{2} = a\left[\cos\omega t + \cos(\omega t + \phi)\right]\)
Using the identity \(\cos C + \cos D = 2\cos\dfrac{C + D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C - D}{2}\):
\(y = 2a\cos\dfrac{\phi}{2}\cos\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\)
This is a wave of the same frequency with resultant amplitude
\(A = 2a\cos\dfrac{\phi}{2}\)
Since intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, \(I = kA^{2}\):
\(I = k\left(4a^{2}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right) = 4I_{0}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2}\)
MAXIMUM VALUE. When \(\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2} = 1\), that is \(\phi = 0, 2\pi, 4\pi, \ldots\):
\(I_{max} = 4I_{0}\)
MINIMUM VALUE. When \(\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2} = 0\), that is \(\phi = \pi, 3\pi, \ldots\):
\(I_{min} = 0\)
Energy is not created or destroyed by this: the average of \(4I_{0}\cos^{2}\dfrac{\phi}{2}\) over all phases is \(2I_{0}\), exactly the sum of the two separate intensities. Interference REDISTRIBUTES the light rather than adding to it.
(ii) (I) FIRST ORDER MINIMUM. The minima of a single-slit pattern lie at \(a\sin\theta = n\lambda\), giving
\(y_{n} = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{a}\)
With \(n = 1\), \(\lambda = 600\) nm, \(D = 1{\cdot}5\) m and \(a = 3\ \mathrm{mm} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\) m:
\(y_{1} = \dfrac{600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1{\cdot}5}{3 \times 10^{-3}} = 3 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}\)
The first minimum lies \(0{\cdot}3\) mm from the centre.
(II) SECOND ORDER MAXIMUM. The secondary maxima lie roughly midway between the minima, at \(a\sin\theta = (2n + 1)\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\), giving
\(y_{n} = \dfrac{(2n + 1)\lambda D}{2a}\)
With \(n = 2\):
\(y_{2} = \dfrac{5 \times 600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1{\cdot}5}{2 \times 3 \times 10^{-3}} = 7{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}\)
The second order maximum lies \(0{\cdot}75\) mm from the centre.
Note the contrast with interference, where \(n\lambda\) gives a MAXIMUM: in diffraction the same condition locates a MINIMUM, and that reversal is the commonest error in this topic.
